They moved inside. The tank room hummed—blue LEDs, the faint iodine note of clean brine.

Signe snapped a refractometer shut. “We’re sitting high. Thirty-three point four. Temp is nine. That difference is stressing the film.”

“That film is our stability,” Einar said. “If we drop fast, we slough it.”

“We won’t drop fast,” Alma said. “Half-degree per hour. Point-two PSU per adjustment. Setpoint eight degrees, thirty-two even.”

Signe nodded. “Copy. I’ll trim with RO, not dilution. Gentle.”

Einar’s fingers hovered over valves. “Say it again so I don’t wear it.”

“Valve B to quarter,” Signe said. “RO at thirty percent. Skim pump stays. No backflush.”

He eased the handle. The manifold changed pitch.

Alma watched the data creep. “Thirty-three point two. Nine becomes eight point nine.”

“Culture looks intact,” Signe murmured, peering through the port. “No floc.”

Einar exhaled. “Dock again in twenty?”

“Ten,” Alma said. “We’re aiming for clean. No skær on the menu, no surprises.”

Signe tapped the log. “New parameters: temp eight, salinity thirty-two. Set.”

Heat lamps hummed. The pass glowed like a sandbar.

“Herring’s at eight degrees. Brine rinse is clean,” Signe said, setting a tray.

Alma lifted a fillet, silver tight as lacquer. “Course one up. Raw herring, whey, rye oil, vinegar steam.”

“Table six asked if this is the one,” a server said, breath quick.

“It’s not,” Alma said. “Tell them it’s the sea without tricks.”

Plates flowed. The dining room murmured—linen hush, glass clicks. A diner leaned forward. “We heard about the…hit.”

Signe met his eye with a small smile. “You’ll taste the harbor. That’s all.”

At the pass, Alma checked a spoon. “Onion ice is dry?”

“Feather-dry,” Signe said. “No drift.”

“Send.”

Second course landed: warm herring rib, cabbage ash, dill seed. A fork paused, then cut. Someone exhaled. Someone nodded.

“Salt reads thirty-two even,” Signe murmured, glancing at the tiny meter clipped to her jacket. “We’re stable.”

“Keep it there.”

A server returned. “Table nine says the texture is…exact.”

“Good,” Alma said. “Third: smoked backbone tea. Pour at the table.”

By dessert—buckwheat, whey caramel—the room had settled into soft, satisfied talk.

Modest claps rose from two-tops. A diner stood, shook Alma’s hand. “It’s clear,” he said simply.

“Thank you,” she replied. “That’s all we wanted.”

Glass walls held a winter-blue sky; snow crusted the harbor cranes beyond. Inside, a conference hall hummed like a cooled engine—espresso hiss, hushed shoes on carpet.

“The LOIs read as agreed,” said the lead investor, cufflinks like tiny suns. “Exclusive territory, perpetual license back, audit rights.”

Kaspar signed the first page without looking up. “Deliverables tied to openings, not seasons.”

“Our IP clause,” a lawyer said, tapping. “All formulations, methods, coordinates—proprietary to the venture.”

“Coordinates?” Petra’s laugh was polished chrome. “You want to trademark a tide?”

The investor smiled pleasantly. “We’re protecting value.”

Kaspar turned the pen in his fingers. “We brand the experience; sourcing notes stay internal.”

“Then sign the NDA,” the lawyer replied, sliding a stack. “No public reference to origin, suppliers, or lab protocols. Ten-year tail.”

Petra leaned toward Kaspar. “You’re building a museum with velvet ropes.”

“I’m building a network,” he said. He initialed, page after page. The pen whispered; the room cooled further.

A junior associate angled an iPad. “Dubai principals are on.”

A square of faces flickered. “Welcome,” Kaspar said. “We’re aligned.”

“Final signatures?” the lead asked.

Kaspar exhaled. “Final.” He signed. The lawyer gathered the papers like thin ice, and the investor extended a hand. “To clarity,” he said. Kaspar shook it. “To control,” Petra murmured.

Kaspar stood by the ficus, lobby light cold on marble. Suitcases hushed past. Counsel hovered, tablet bright, a finger on a clause.

He called. “Alma.”

“Say it fast. I’m between prep and staff meal.”

“NDAs tighten. Across all ventures. Sourcing is internal language only. Ten-year tail.”

Silence. Coffee cups clinked somewhere.

“You’re gagging the sea,” Alma said. “I need to publish beds and limits. That’s the point.”

Counsel leaned in, whispering. Kaspar relayed. “Origin descriptors allowed—region, not coordinates. Supplier names are restricted.”

“That’s not transparency. That’s a brochure.”

“We can’t let competitors walk our maps.”

“It’s not a map; it’s stewardship,” Alma said. “We’re naming pressure, not selling postcards.”

A man in linen asked Kaspar for a pen; he waved him off. “Dubai signed on this basis. It’s uniform.”

“I won’t lock Signe’s charts in a safe.”

“Then annotate without pins,” Kaspar said. “Make it narrative.”

“That’s spin.”

Counsel tapped the tablet. “Drafts go tonight,” Kaspar said. “Redlines due tomorrow.”

“I won’t hide sources,” Alma said. “Not after what happened.”

Kaspar watched the revolving door sweep a woman out into glare. “You want reach,” he said. “This is the cost.”

“No,” Alma said. “It’s the receipt. I’m not signing it.”

They breathed. Lobby air-conditioning thrummed.

“Drafts incoming,” Kaspar said.

“Send them,” Alma said, and hung up.

Supermoon squatted on the water like a coin. Frost skinned the slip. Alma’s breath smoked as she shoved the bow off.

“Lines,” Einar said, voice flat with focus. Mateo tossed the stern free; Leif sprang in, boots thudding.

A RIB snarled two slips over—Petra’s crew, orange helmets, wake already shouldering.

“Go,” Alma snapped.

Einar feathered throttle, then punched it. The skiff leapt, slapped hard. Spray knifed their faces.

“Chop’s building,” Mateo shouted, braced over the crate.

“We ride it,” Einar said. “Bow up half.”

Leif wiped his glasses with the hem of his cap. “That’s Petra.”

Alma didn’t look. “Hold northwest seam. Bridge skerry off the pylons.”

A crosswave kicked; the hull shuddered. She dropped to a knee, hand on the gunwale, tasting salt. The moon burned a path through broken water.

“Speed or we lose lane,” Mateo said.

“Speed,” Alma answered. “We’re not drifting for her.”

Einar trimmed. The motor climbed in pitch; they skipped over the next set clean. Petra’s RIB hit wrong, buried its nose, threw spray and curses into the air.

“Mark buoy,” Leif called. “Two lengths!”

Alma jabbed ahead. “On my left. We take it.”

The skiff knifed past the buoy. The gap opened. The bridge rose black and close. They had the lead.

Spray burned their cheeks. The bridge pylons loomed like cold ribs. Dawn bled under the supermoon, turning the chop into hammered copper.

Petra’s RIB surged back into their wake. A horn barked—two blasts, then a long, angry third.

“Starboard vessel has right of way!” a voice bawled across the water—Petra’s captain, tinny through a loudhailer.

“Not in a narrow channel,” Einar muttered. “We’re inside line.”

Another horn. “Give way!”

Alma stood, hand on the console rail. “Hold course. Take the lee of the western pylon.”

Mateo set his feet. “We thread that, we’re in rock wash.”

“We thread it.”

Leif squinted through spray. “Skerry’s up—white lick, ten o’clock.”

The RIB clawed closer, throwing square waves off its bow. “You cut me off and I file,” the captain shouted. “You hear me?”

Alma cupped her mouth. “Mark your distance.”

Einar dropped a fraction of throttle, then snapped it. Their skiff hopped the RIB’s wake, slid into the pylon’s wind shadow. Water smoothed. The skerry showed teeth—a slab ringed with froth.

“Line ready,” Alma said.

Mateo swung the boat hook. Leif grabbed the painter. Einar kissed the hull against the rock.

Boots hit stone. Alma leapt first, rope in hand, salt in her lungs. “We’re on.”

Boot soles scraped barnacle. The skerry’s skin stank of metal and rot.

Alma crouched at the lip of a tide pool. The skær beds were raked open, tufts ripped like hair from a comb. Bright plastic flags—Petra’s—stabbed into drill holes along the spine of the rock.

“Jesus,” Leif said, breath white. “It looks shaved.”

Mateo knelt, fingers hovering. “Not raked. Cut. See the edges?” He traced a clean crescent. “Blade. Multiple passes. Fast.”

Alma touched a stump. It bled brine. “How many markers?”

Leif counted, jaw tight. “Twelve. She grid-mapped it.”

Mateo pulled a caliper from his jacket, measured a wound. “Three centimeters deep. That’s into the holdfast. It won’t throw new growth from that.”

“Don’t say won’t,” Alma said, though her voice thinned.

Leif straightened, eyes on the horizon, then back down at the flags. “We came to harvest. Are we… harvesting?”

Mateo shook his head. “Not from this bed.”

Alma stood, wet to the knees. “No pulls. We catalog.”

Leif splayed a sample bag, swallowing. “I’ll photo each scar. You log coordinates?”

Mateo nodded, already tapping his phone. “Depth, cut angle, density.”

Alma moved along the rock, tugging a flag free. The stem squealed in the hole. “We halt,” she said. “We count what’s left.”

Spray licked the ridge as Alma and Einar climbed the seam of rock. Petra’s flags winked like candy in a bruise.

Einar crouched, glove on the nearest stake. “She drilled this. Fresh dust. See the chalking?”

“See the theft,” Alma said, flat. Her breath smoked in the wind.

He lifted his phone, shot the hole, the flag, the cut edge. “Careful with words.”

“I’m not posting,” Alma said. “I’m remembering.”

Einar angled to the next scar, clicking. “Angles, depth, distances. We say what is here. Not who.”

“She signed the plastic,” Alma said. He flicked the tag; PETRA, black marker, smudged with salt.

“Photograph the letters. Don’t say them.” He swept the ridge with the rangefinder. “Give me grid start.”

Alma read the handheld. “55.6792, 12.6038.” Her voice stayed even. “Datum WGS84.”

He repeated it into the mic, then, “Offset two meters east. Next.”

They moved in a tight cadence: photo, note, coordinate. Alma pulled one flag, slid it into a bag without comment. The stem squealed against the rock like a rebuke.

“Count of markers?” Einar asked.

“Twelve on the spine, three below the lip.”

He nodded, eyes narrowed against the glare, and took a wide frame of the ridge. “Last set. Then we send the packet.”

“We send the facts,” Alma said.

“Exactly.” He logged the final point and saved.

Late morning glare flattened the skerry, the water slapping like slow applause. Alma knelt at the edge where the last green clung in a crescent.

“Don’t,” Freja said, voice tight. “We touch it, we’re part of it.”

“We’re part of it either way,” Alma answered, sliding the scalpel from its sleeve. “Archival only. One gram.”

Mateo held the meter, numbers flickering. “Salinity logged. Coordinates match Einar’s grid.”

Einar opened the hard case. “Bag 31-A. Seal 743226.” His tone was clerical, grave.

Alma pinched a tuft no bigger than a thumbnail, the blades soft as breath. She cut once, clean, and the rock showed its pale seam. The crew flinched as if it had cried out.

“It looks like theft,” Freja said.

“It looks like record,” Alma said. “Chain begins here.” She slid the tuft into the vial, added brine, capped. “Sample 31-A. Late morning, skerry edge. Witness?”

Mateo took the logbook. “Witness Mateo Cruz. Time eleven twenty-three.” He signed. “Custodian?”

“Alma Høy.” She clicked the seal, read the number aloud. Einar repeated it into the recorder.

Freja hesitated, then pressed her initials beside the line. “I don’t want my fear to erase facts.”

“Measured, then,” Alma said, handing the sealed vial to Einar. “Custody transfer.”

“Received,” he said, tucking it into foam. “Chain started.”

The RIB slapped the noon chop, city mirage wavering ahead. Alma stood at the bow rail, hair salt-stiff, and raised her voice over the motor.

“No more cuts,” she said. “Effective now. Moratorium stands until beds recover. We serve without skær.”

Freja exhaled like she’d been bracing all morning. “Say it louder for my hands.”

“No. More. Cuts.”

Mateo flicked off the meter. “Bookings are pegged on that course. We’re about to bleed.”

“We bleed clean,” Alma said. “Principle over revenue.”

Einar closed the hard case around the single vial. “Policy needs ink.”

“Write it,” Alma said. “Publish the numbers, the limit zero, the why. Put my name on it.”

A deckhand, Rune, glanced back from the tiller. “Kaspar’s going to torch us.”

“Kaspar doesn’t run the tide,” Alma said. “We’re done taking what can’t give back.”

Freja leaned on the gunwale, eyes on the water. “Then we cook absence. We cook the hole it leaves.”

“We cook what’s left,” Alma said. “And we pay people through it.”

Mateo met her glare, then nodded once. “I’ll rewrite HACCP, pull the pairing, reflow prep.”

Einar lifted his phone, thumbed the note. “Moratorium. Noon today. Signed Alma Høy.”

“Add this,” Alma said. “If a guest asks why, we tell them.”

Rune cracked a grin. “Policy set.”

“Policy set,” Alma repeated, and the motor carried it home.

Candles bowed in the draft as the dining room breathed between courses. Alma stepped to the pass, jaw set. “Fire two ‘Return.’” She tapped a rubber-banded stack. “Cards go with it.”

Freja hesitated. “Kaspar hasn’t—”

“He doesn’t run the tide,” Alma said. “Go.”

Kaspar slid in from the doorway, cufflinks catching tea light. “Alma. We do not disclose mid-service.”

“We do tonight,” she replied, handing Mateo a stack. “Table twelve first.”

“It is not approved.” Kaspar’s smile pressed thin. “You will hold.”

Mateo glanced between them. “Chef?”

“Truth on the plate,” Alma said. “Truth on the card.”

Kaspar leaned close. “You jeopardize the brand.”

“You jeopardize nothing by telling them what’s in their mouths.” Alma turned to the line. “Walk.”

Servers glided. Porcelain kissed linen. Next to the bowls, white cards landed, crisp as new shells.

A diner at twelve read aloud, brow knitting. “Moratorium?”

A couple at six traded cards. “No skær?”

“Chef,” a server whispered, “they’re asking why.”

“Because we took too much,” Alma said, stepping into the room. “And we’ve stopped.”

Kaspar’s jaw worked. “This is insubordination.”

“It’s accountability,” Alma said, and placed the last card herself.

Murmurs spread, low and tidal.

The office behind the kitchen hummed like a walk-in: steel, invoices, a thin pane of glass vibrating with the pass. Kaspar shut the door. “Get Frandsen on,” he told his phone. “Now.”

A click, then a dry voice. “Kaspar.”

“She has breached. Activate clawbacks. Freeze operations.”

Alma slipped in, flecked with steam. “You’re freezing who? The fishmonger? My dishwasher?”

Frandsen: “Notice of breach, clause twelve. We suspend disbursements and lock operational accounts pending cure.”

“Do it,” Kaspar said, eyes cold. “Also circulate an NDA reminder: disclosure is unauthorized.”

Alma leaned on the filing cabinet. “Our mission was to stop harm. I stopped it.”

“Our mission is solvency,” Kaspar replied. “You chose theater.”

Einar knocked, half in. “Chef—front asks if dessert is still—”

Kaspar didn’t look at him. “Tell the team payroll pauses until compliance. Any service under Alma’s ‘Return’ is off-policy. Personal liability attaches if you assist.”

Einar swallowed. “So—go home?”

“Finish the course,” Alma said, voice low. “We feed them.”

Frandsen: “Kaspar, I’m queuing the freeze. Vendors notified. Staff to receive warning letters.”

Kaspar nodded. “Send them.”

Alma exhaled, steady. “Then I’ll read the card again.”

Candles guttered as chairs scraped. A quarter of the room stood, then another cluster. Coats slid from hooks like a hush.

“At this point, we should go,” a man said, napkin folded like a surrender.

His partner kept her seat. “I want to hear her. We came to taste honesty.”

Alma stepped to the threshold of the dining room, hands clean, apron damp. “For those who stay: eelgrass broth, toasted rye oil, lemon peel. No skær. We’ll finish what we can.”

A server—Ingrid—lifted a tray. “Table six, bowls coming hot.”

A woman near the window glanced at the exit, then back at Alma. “Will the staff be paid?”

“We’ll take care of each other,” Alma said. “Eat while it’s warm.”

Half the room settled. The rest filed out, murmuring apologies that felt like drafts under a door.

Ingrid set a bowl before an elderly diner. Steam carried a seaside sweetness. He cupped it, eyes wet. “Smells like ferry mornings,” he said. “That’s enough.”

At the corner banquette, a young cook ladled carefully. “We’re okay?” he whispered.

“We’re here,” Alma replied.

Spoons touched porcelain. Conversation thinned to soft clinks. The line sent more bowls. The room, halved, held. Service moved, smaller, steady.

Steam thinned to a sheen at the pass when two jackets with crests stepped in. The taller one lifted a wallet. “Regulatory Affairs. End of service?”

Alma wiped her hands. “Almost. You’ll get what you need. Please speak plainly.”

“Records of sourcing, processing, and the recirculating tank,” the woman said. “HACCP, supplier logs, discharge notes. Tonight’s service sheet.”

Einar slid a clipboard from beneath the heat lamp, pages corner-clipped. “Prep lists, temps, corrective actions. The catch-limits board is current.”

She scanned, pen ticking. “Supplier?”

Signe stepped forward, tide-stained notebook in her palm. “Coordinates, pulls, closures. Supply halted. Here.” She laid the notebook flat, a small square of salt on the cover.

“And the tank?” the taller one asked.

Alma nodded to Einar. He set a clearly labeled folder on the stainless. “Install photos, salinity readings, maintenance, and… a statement.” He didn’t look away.

“We’ll collect copies,” the woman said, voice even. “We’ll also need staff rosters and training attestations.”

“I’ll print them now,” Alma said. “Guests are finishing bowls.”

“We won’t impede,” the man replied. He checked a calendar. “Inspection, nine tomorrow. Access to the premises and all storage.”

“Granted,” Alma said.

The woman capped her pen. “Thank you. Accountability starts here.”

“It does,” Alma answered, handing over the stapled sets.

The test kitchen was all hum and tile. Mateo slid a tray forward. “Version eight. No skær.”

Leif leaned in, eyes level with the steam. “How many bubbles before the break?”

“Four, then a sigh,” Mateo said, counting under his breath.

Alma watched Leif’s hands hover. “You don’t have to do this.”

“I do,” Leif said. “Reset the torch. I want the caramel edge thinner.”

They ran it again. He tapped the ramekin, listened to the skin. “Forty seconds shorter.” He tasted, blinked, waited for a ghost that didn’t come. “Acid needs a nudge.”

“Sea buckthorn or fermented currant?” Mateo asked.

“Currant. Less shout.”

Alma spooned the broth around the kohlrabi ribbons, a quiet pool. “Texture’s the story now.”

“It always was,” Leif said, softer than he meant. He lifted a slice, watched light slide over it, then nodded. “Lock this. Course three.”

Mateo scribbled. “Locked.”

Leif took the notebook from his pocket, wrote without lifting his head. Alma leaned. “What are you calling it?”

“In absence,” he said. “Not as loss. As frame.”

She exhaled. “Then we serve the frame.”

He set the pen down, steady. “Run it from the top.”

Leif sat at the staff table under the bruised cone of the exit light. The hall was a held breath. He clicked his pen twice, then spoke to the empty chairs as if they needed convincing.

“Course one,” he said, writing. “Not aroma. Approach. Steam like a coat you don’t wear, just let brush past. Say: ‘You’ll hear the broth before you taste it.’”

He paused, sniffed nothing, smiled anyway. “No perfume. Texture. Give them verbs.”

He scratched: snap, sigh, yield.

“Course two,” he murmured. “The kohlrabi holds a glare like ice on a pond. Tell them: ‘Angle your spoon so the ribbon skates.’”

He tapped the ramekin, listening for the thin drum of sugar. “Skin talks,” he said. “Say: ‘Crack with the side, not the tip—let it break as if on its own.’”

He tried the word bright, crossed it out, wrote clear. “Acid isn’t a shout; it’s a tilt,” he dictated. “Currant tilts. Sea buckthorn yanks. We tilt.”

He stacked the pages, numbered them, then rewrote each as a cue.

“Server: place, pause, ask, wait.”

He underlined wait twice.

At the bottom, he printed a title: In Absence — Service Language.

He set the pen on top, centered the stack, and let the room have its quiet.

The municipal chamber hummed with radiator heat and stacked binders. A clerk swore in Signe.

Panel Chair: Ms. Leth, supply records show increased pulls.

Signe: I cut quotas in November. I halted supply when I saw torn beds. Coordinates stayed closed per my policy, not Mr. Kaspar’s NDAs.

Kaspar’s Counsel: Objection to characterization. My client sought innovation within industry norms.

Panel Member Two: The unlicensed recirculating tank?

Counsel: A pilot apparatus. Temporary. No demonstrable harm linked—

Einar: Backflush timestamps match the harbor closure. I filed video. The pump restart was ordered over protest.

Chair: Mr. Hald, you were operations lead?

Einar: I ran prep and logs. I flagged the tank in December. When the squall hit, Mateo said stop. We were told push.

Counsel: Individual staff contradicted procedures, exposing the company.

Alma: I ended skær service and published limits. The tank was Kaspar’s install. I didn’t authorize a harbor feed.

Panel Member One: Documentation?

Alma: HACCP amendment, tide board policy, dated. Submitted.

Chair: Thank you. Findings will address the tank’s status, discharge negligence, and stewardship compliance.

The panel bent over their screens. The clerk typed steadily. The Chair lifted a stamped sheet.

Chair: Draft findings prepared. Distribution to parties now.

The Chair adjusted her glasses. “Findings: administrative fines for discharge negligence and unlicensed apparatus. Order: the recirculating tank is to be dismantled and removed within seven days. Disposal by a licensed contractor. Independent audit filed within fourteen.”

Kaspar’s Counsel half-rose. “We note our objection to causality—”

“Noted and overruled,” Panel Member Two said. “Public harm, operational breach.”

Alma exhaled. “We’ll comply. Service will run without the tank.”

Panel Member One scrolled. “Stewardship: The panel adopts the Signe/DTU protocol as binding—published coordinates, seasonal closures, and catch limits.”

Signe blinked, then nodded. “I’ll post the charts by tomorrow. DTU will monitor beds and publish monthly.”

“Funding obligations?” Counsel snapped.

“Shared,” the Chair said. “Operator funds monitoring; DTU maintains data. Noncompliance escalates penalties.”

Einar whispered, “We’ll need new prep flows.”

Alma: “We’ll write them tonight.”

Panel Member Two tapped the page. “Compliance timeline: seven days for dismantle; fourteen for audit; thirty for full stewardship implementation; ninety for community report-back in this chamber.”

Signe’s pen scratched an X in her notebook. “I’ll convene the fishers in a week.”

The clerk stamped the last sheet. The radiator ticked. The Chair held up the order. “This restores the water. You have your dates. See that you keep them.”

Ring lights burned the studio kitchen into a mirror. Petra held a jade blender pitcher up to camera. “We’re done chasing skær,” she said. “We’re doing plant-based memory.”

The social lead lifted a brow. “Meaning… flavor plus prompt? Or—”

“Meaning no algae, no scandal,” Petra cut in. “Memory is a texture. We’ll engineer it.”

Food stylist misted a tray of glossed kohlrabi coins; a PA dragged a fake window into frame. The DP: “Say the line again. Slower.”

Petra smiled to lens, lacquer-slick. “Plant. Based. Memory.”

Copywriter hovered with a laptop. “Tagline options: ‘Recall Without Harm,’ ‘Grow What You Remember,’ ‘Memory, Cultivated.’”

“‘Grow What You Remember,’” Petra said. “Stamp it.”

The R&D intern whispered, “But there’s no trigger compound. It’s agar and aromatics—”

“It’s a ritual,” Petra said, placing a spoon in the shot. “Ritual is repeatable. Repeatability is scale.”

“B-roll of hands,” the DP called. “Pour. Steam curl. Tilt.”

An assistant wafted dill vapor through a copper funnel. Phones captured vertical. The social lead nodded, already cutting a Reel. “Launch grid: nine squares, one carousel, one BTS. Hashtag ‘#PlantBasedMemory.’”

Petra set the bowl down in its hero light. “Frame it,” she said. “Then publish.”

“Lights to half,” Alma said. The smaller floor breathed—a dozen bare tables, no linen, a chalked tide board in Einar’s tidy block, and a laminated harbor map with pinned coordinates and red-limit rings.

Einar tapped the board. “Low slack at 19:12. We run the eelgrass broth then. After that, no shore herbs.”

Freja tied her apron tighter. “Feels monkish.”

“Feels honest,” Alma said. She slid a small envelope to each person. “Back pay for the pause. Full hours.”

Mateo glanced up. “You sure?”

“I’m sure.”

Behind the pass, the printer coughed once, shy. A single ticket. Then another, spaced like slow rain.

“Walk-in?” a server said, hopeful.

“No,” Alma smiled. “Reservation—two. Table three.”

Einar posted tonight’s pulls on a clip: eelgrass, mussel liquor, last of the cellar carrots. “We publish, we keep,” he said. “Simple.”

“Simple is expensive,” Freja murmured, counting forks.

Alma wiped the edge of a bowl. “Solvency is a course, too. We serve it warm.”

The door opened; a couple entered, jackets damp, eyes curious. The room gathered itself.

“Fire one broth,” Alma said, calm as tide. “And remind them: coordinates are on the wall.”

“Two broths up,” Einar called, fingertip tapping the tide board. “Low slack passed. Shore herbs closed.”

At the pass, the couple leaned toward the chalk. “You actually put the spots on the wall?” the man asked.

“We did,” Alma said. “Red rings are no-go after pull.”

“So that’s it? No skær course?” the woman said, scanning the limits.

“That’s it tonight,” Einar answered. “Bed needs a week. We wrote it there so you don’t have to guess.”

The man frowned. “We booked for the… you know.”

“You booked for dinner,” Alma said, steady. “You’ll get dinner.”

They tasted the eelgrass broth. The woman’s shoulders dropped. “It’s so clean.”

“Can’t you just… do a small pull?” the man tried.

Einar pointed to the board. “Coordinates, limits, time. We don’t bend those. If we run out, we say so.”

A table of four waved a menu. “You’re out of the mussel toast already?”

“Three orders left,” Mateo called. “After that, we switch to carrot ends with liquor.”

The four traded looks. “Fine. Two now, two carrots next.”

“Thank you,” Alma said. “We pace with the water, not the book.”

Tickets came slow, then even. The room eased into the rhythm. No one rushed. The board held.
